:::{#thm-det-eigenvalues}
#### The determinant of a symmetric matrix is the product of its eigenvalues

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix with real entries,
with eigendecomposition $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Eigvals}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
(@def-eigendecomposition)
and eigenvalues $\eigval_1, \ldots, \eigval_p$
on the diagonal of $\matr{\Eigvals}$.
Then

$$
\det(\matr{A}) = \prod_{i=1}^p \eigval_i.
$$

:::

::: proof

First, $\det(\tp{\matr{Q}})\det(\matr{Q}) = 1$:

$$
\ba
\det(\tp{\matr{Q}})\det(\matr{Q})
&= \det(\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q})
&& \text{(determinant of a product)}
\\
&= \det(\matr{I}_p)
&& \text{(} \matr{Q} \text{ is orthogonal)}
\\
&= 1
&& \text{(determinant of the identity)}
\ea
$$

Then:

$$
\ba
\det(\matr{A})
&= \det(\matr{Q}\matr{\Eigvals}\tp{\matr{Q}})
&& \text{(substitute the eigendecomposition)}
\\
&= \det(\matr{Q}) \det(\matr{\Eigvals}) \det(\tp{\matr{Q}})
&& \text{(determinant of a product, twice)}
\\
&= \det(\matr{\Eigvals}) \cd \det(\tp{\matr{Q}})\det(\matr{Q})
&& \text{(reorder the three numbers)}
\\
&= \det(\matr{\Eigvals})
&& \text{(the first display)}
\\
&= \prod_{i=1}^p \eigval_i
&& \text{(determinant of a diagonal matrix)}
\ea
$$

The product steps are @thm-det-product,
the orthogonality step is @def-orthogonal-matrix,
and the identity and diagonal steps are @thm-det-diagonal and @exm-det-diagonal.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-det-pd}
#### A positive definite matrix has a positive determinant

If $\matr{A}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite),
then $\det(\matr{A}) > 0$.

:::

::: proof

By @thm-definite-eigenvalues, every eigenvalue of $\matr{A}$ is positive,
so their product, which is $\det(\matr{A})$ by @thm-det-eigenvalues,
is positive.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-det-eigenvalues}
#### Two ways to the same determinant

$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
has eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ (@exm-eigenvalue),
so @thm-det-eigenvalues gives $\det(\matr{A}) = 3 \cd 1 = 3$,
matching $2 \cd 2 - 1 \cd 1 = 3$ from @exm-determinant.

:::
